# Day 4 — Overview {#sec-day4}

Days 1 to 3 predicted a number and scored it with an average error. Today the
outcome is a class — this patient has diabetes or does not — and two things
change. The model stops emitting a prediction and starts emitting a
*probability*; and somebody, at some point, has to turn that probability into an
action. That second step is not part of the model, it is not chosen by the
software, and it is where most of the clinical consequences live. @sec-pipeline
ended with a loose end that today picks up: a decision is not a prediction.

Along the way we stop hand-writing each model's own syntax and move to the two
frameworks the rest of the module uses, `tidymodels` and `scikit-learn`.

## Objectives

By the end of the day you should be able to, without looking anything up:

::: {.objective-list}
- Fit, swap and score a classifier through one interface in either language,
  and say which line changes the algorithm, which changes the engine and which
  changes the preprocessing.
- Convert freely between a probability, its odds and its log-odds, and read an
  odds ratio off a logistic regression coefficient.
- Build a confusion table at a stated threshold, and say in patients — not
  percentages — what moving that threshold buys and what it costs.
- Justify a threshold from a stated ratio of the cost of a missed case to the
  cost of a false alarm, and say why 0.5 is not that justification.
:::

## What you need before you start

- R and Python working locally, and this project open in your editor
  (@sec-setup). Today needs `tidymodels`, `glmnet` and `ranger` on the R side
  and `scikit-learn` on the Python side; `check_setup()` will tell you.
- `data/diabetes.csv`, which is the day's only dataset. It is the synthetic
  replacement for the withdrawn Pima Indians data and its values are not the
  published ones — @sec-data-diabetes explains why, and it matters the moment
  you compare a number here with a number in a textbook.
- The habit from @sec-pipeline of asking what a model is being compared
  *against*. Today's baseline is not the mean; it is the commonest class, and it
  is a much harder opponent than it looks.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Running the day.** 4.1 is the only exercise that is mostly scaffolding, and
it is tempting to cut it; do not, because 4.3 relies on its fixed every-fifth-row
split and on students having seen that scikit-learn penalises by default. Check
before the session that `glmnet` and `ranger` are installed — a missing engine
package fails at `fit()`, not at the specification, which confuses everyone.

**Where the time actually goes.** 4.1 Task 3 (the workflow and the Pipeline)
always overruns; it is the first time most students have built either. 4.2 is
the fastest of the three and can absorb the overrun. 4.3 Task 1 should be
counted by hand even by students who know `conf_mat()`, because the trap later
on the page is exactly that function.

**Plenary.** The one thing that should be said aloud by a student rather than by
you: that a model at its default threshold was beaten, on cost, by investigating
every patient in the test set. If nobody says it, 4.3's third numbered point is
the script.

**What carries forward.** Today deliberately reports only counts, sensitivity,
specificity, PPV and accuracy, and deliberately avoids ROC and AUC — those are
@sec-classification-metrics, and they land better once students have chosen a
threshold by hand and disliked the experience.
